summary:
Tlaxcala stands under Mexico's national framework and adds its own state statute on top of it. The state congress's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and the decree text is published on the state congress's own site. The procedure requires no court proceeding, which is the legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update identity documents in Tlaxcala.

The state's civil-union law took effect on 12 January 2017, giving Tlaxcala a state-level partnership status that rests on a separate instrument from the 2019 recognition decree.
tangentialFactors: Tlaxcala's civil-union law, in force since 12 January 2017, predates the 2019 gender-recognition decree by two years. The two operate as distinct instruments, so a visitor relying on one does not automatically engage the other.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tlaxcala use the state Civil Code procedure created by Decree D.113 to change name and gender marker. The decree is published by the state congress, so the procedure's terms are readable at source rather than only through secondary description.

The state's civil-union law has been in force since 12 January 2017.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory holds no Tlaxcala-specific record of how the 2019 procedure operates in practice. Processing times, fees, refusal rates, and whether the procedure extends to minors are not sourced.

No Tlaxcala-specific incident, prosecution, hate-crime enforcement, or protection measure appears in the inventory.
